Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code.
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft)
Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement Actions on Objectives High
psexec / paexec / smbexec / wmic /node — service install over SMB from remote host.
ATT&CKT1021.002 T1569.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
   or (FileName =~ "wmic.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "/node:")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc

SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688            // process-create (audit-policy required)
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\psexec.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\psexesvc.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\paexec.exe"
   or (NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe" and CommandLine has "/node:")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: PsExec / SMB Lateral Movement Tooling Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d03
status: experimental
description: |
    PsExec, paexec, smbexec, csexec, remcom — admin-grade tooling that
    pivots over SMB. Pair with `wmic /node:` for the full cluster.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1021/002/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1569/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1021.002
    - attack.t1569.002
    - attack.lateral-movement
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_psexec:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\psexec.exe'
            - '\psexec64.exe'
            - '\psexesvc.exe'
            - '\paexec.exe'
            - '\csexec.exe'
            - '\remcom.exe'
            - '\smbexec.py'
    selection_wmic_remote:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\wmic.exe'
        CommandLine|contains:
            - '/node:'
    condition: selection_psexec or selection_wmic_remote
falsepositives:
    - Sysadmins running approved remote-management tooling — wrap with
      a known-admin-host watchlist
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
       OR (Processes.process_name="wmic.exe" AND Processes.process="*/node:*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
       OR (Processes.process_name="wmic.exe" AND Processes.process="*/node:*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: LSASS Process Access Outside Microsoft-Signed Tooling
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d04
status: experimental
description: |
    Anything opening lsass.exe with read-memory access that isn't a
    Microsoft signed component (Defender, csrss, etc.) is suspect.
    Mimikatz / Pypykatz / nanodump signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1003.001
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: process_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        TargetImage|endswith: '\lsass.exe'
    filter_known_good:
        SourceImage|endswith:
            - '\MsSense.exe'
            - '\MsMpEng.exe'
            - '\csrss.exe'
            - '\svchost.exe'
            - '\wininit.exe'
            - '\services.exe'
            - '\lsm.exe'
            - '\SearchProtocolHost.exe'
    condition: selection and not filter_known_good
falsepositives:
    - Third-party EDR / forensic tools — extend the filter list
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard Installation High
ConnectWise / AnyDesk / TeamViewer / ScreenConnect / Atera installed outside IT change windows = common tradecraft for ransomware affiliates and IT-helpdesk impersonators.
ATT&CKT1219
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("AnyDesk.exe","TeamViewer.exe","TeamViewer_Service.exe",
        "ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe","ConnectWiseControl.ClientService.exe",
        "atera_agent.exe","SplashtopStreamer.exe","RustDesk.exe","NinjaOne.exe")
   or FileName matches regex @"(?i)kaseya.*\.exe"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\AnyDesk.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\TeamViewer.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\TeamViewer_Service.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\ConnectWiseControl.ClientService.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\atera_agent.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\SplashtopStreamer.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\RustDesk.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\NinjaOne.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName,

| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Scheduled Task Creation with Suspicious Image / Encoded Args
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d0d
status: experimental
description: |
    schtasks.exe /create with payload-shaped action — points at

        OR Processes.process="*rundll32*" OR Processes.process="*-enc*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*\Users\Public*"
        OR Processes.process="*\AppData\*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

DeviceProcessEvents

| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"

| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName,
          CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("22b38dad7da097ea03aa28d0614164cd25fafeb1383dbc15047e34c8050f6f67", "fe1033335a045c696c900d435119d210361966e2fb5cd1ba3382608cfa2c8e68", "078163d5c16f64caa5a14784323fd51451b8c831c73396b967b4e35e6879937b") or SHA1 in~ ("22b38dad7da097ea03aa28d0614164cd25fafeb1383dbc15047e34c8050f6f67", "fe1033335a045c696c900d435119d210361966e2fb5cd1ba3382608cfa2c8e68", "078163d5c16f64caa5a14784323fd51451b8c831c73396b967b4e35e6879937b") or MD5 in~ ("22b38dad7da097ea03aa28d0614164cd25fafeb1383dbc15047e34c8050f6f67", "fe1033335a045c696c900d435119d210361966e2fb5cd1ba3382608cfa2c8e68", "078163d5c16f64caa5a14784323fd51451b8c831c73396b967b4e35e6879937b")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("22b38dad7da097ea03aa28d0614164cd25fafeb1383dbc15047e34c8050f6f67", "fe1033335a045c696c900d435119d210361966e2fb5cd1ba3382608cfa2c8e68", "078163d5c16f64caa5a14784323fd51451b8c831c73396b967b4e35e6879937b") or SHA1 in~ ("22b38dad7da097ea03aa28d0614164cd25fafeb1383dbc15047e34c8050f6f67", "fe1033335a045c696c900d435119d210361966e2fb5cd1ba3382608cfa2c8e68", "078163d5c16f64caa5a14784323fd51451b8c831c73396b967b4e35e6879937b") or MD5 in~ ("22b38dad7da097ea03aa28d0614164cd25fafeb1383dbc15047e34c8050f6f67", "fe1033335a045c696c900d435119d210361966e2fb5cd1ba3382608cfa2c8e68", "078163d5c16f64caa5a14784323fd51451b8c831c73396b967b4e35e6879937b")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["22b38dad7da097ea03aa28d0614164cd25fafeb1383dbc15047e34c8050f6f67", "fe1033335a045c696c900d435119d210361966e2fb5cd1ba3382608cfa2c8e68", "078163d5c16f64caa5a14784323fd51451b8c831c73396b967b4e35e6879937b"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.

id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |
    A signed vendor binary (in the article's named-vendors list)
    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same
    vendor.

            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'

Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("0a8ab3d16b12d3a453ee5a3208fe04744ad54514ef8ea27bb8fe32679efad270", "9c2ce925133a3bf5a924063bbef8df49918d5b7258695c1894cd18c75970157a") or SHA1 in~ ("0a8ab3d16b12d3a453ee5a3208fe04744ad54514ef8ea27bb8fe32679efad270", "9c2ce925133a3bf5a924063bbef8df49918d5b7258695c1894cd18c75970157a") or MD5 in~ ("0a8ab3d16b12d3a453ee5a3208fe04744ad54514ef8ea27bb8fe32679efad270", "9c2ce925133a3bf5a924063bbef8df49918d5b7258695c1894cd18c75970157a")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("0a8ab3d16b12d3a453ee5a3208fe04744ad54514ef8ea27bb8fe32679efad270", "9c2ce925133a3bf5a924063bbef8df49918d5b7258695c1894cd18c75970157a") or SHA1 in~ ("0a8ab3d16b12d3a453ee5a3208fe04744ad54514ef8ea27bb8fe32679efad270", "9c2ce925133a3bf5a924063bbef8df49918d5b7258695c1894cd18c75970157a") or MD5 in~ ("0a8ab3d16b12d3a453ee5a3208fe04744ad54514ef8ea27bb8fe32679efad270", "9c2ce925133a3bf5a924063bbef8df49918d5b7258695c1894cd18c75970157a")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["0a8ab3d16b12d3a453ee5a3208fe04744ad54514ef8ea27bb8fe32679efad270", "9c2ce925133a3bf5a924063bbef8df49918d5b7258695c1894cd18c75970157a"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-48027")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-48027")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc
APPLICATION

Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Trusted Vendor Binary Launching Unusual Children
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |
    A signed vendor binary (in the article's named-vendors list)
    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same
    vendor.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1195
    - attack.initial-access
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\wmic.exe'
            - '\bitsadmin.exe'
    selection_parent_vendor:
        ParentImage|contains:
            - '\Program Files\'
            - '\Program Files (x86)\'
    condition: selection_child and selection_parent_vendor
falsepositives:
    - Many — installers and updaters legitimately spawn children. Pin
      the parent path to specific vendor binaries observed in the
      article before alerting.
level: medium
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

let BadHashes = dynamic(["1a4afce34918bdc74ae3f31edaffffaa0ee074d83618f53edfd88137927340b8", "b0cefb66b953e5184b6adb3035e9e267335ac5eabfe1848e07834777b9397b74", "e7347d90653efc565f03733a95e9209d78f9cfa81e31ff2b2dd9d48d75a4b8b1", "43f2b001846c4966073ebffa5be8f15e491a1e7d32bbd805d57406ff540e0dd9", "cb86f4f223daa54467c7782a0d8607e9c84e2bb633e6f0e51d9a19579e200990", "558b09d7ad0d1660e2a0fb8a06da81a6f42e06d2", "ba642fe2c7c65e42dd7f6444b83023dc6827e08c", "9d88f040c44b5f4d5f9db15ff89310776c168e99", "acfc3f957a63b4cde93ff645f2b6bf26a8ed1bbf"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] Marimo CVE-2026-39987 /terminal/ws RCE: notebook process spawns shell or network tooling Exploitation High
Hunts the initial-access foothold described by Sysdig: an internet-reachable marimo notebook process (Python/uvicorn) spawns sh/bash/curl/wget/nc as a child of the unauthenticated /terminal/ws WebSocket exploit path. The marimo runtime should not be spawning shells or network egress utilities under normal load. Rationale: Anchors on the exact CVE-2026-39987 exploitation chain — marimo Python process spawning a shell/network utility through the unauthenticated /terminal/ws WebSocket. The parent-process predicate (marimo in cmdline of a Python/uvicorn parent) is the article-specific narrowing that distinguishes this from generic Python shellouts. Cross-checked with Sysdig blog and NVD entry confirming /terminal/ws is the exploit primitive. Cross-checked against: • https://webflow.sysdig.com/blog/ai-agent-at-the-wheel-how-an-attacker-used-llms-to-move-from-a-cve-to-an-internal-database-in-4-pivots • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-39987 • https://github.com/Nxploited/CVE-2026-39987
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("python","python3","uvicorn","gunicorn","marimo")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "marimo"
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","curl","wget","ncat","nc","busybox")
    or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/bin/sh","bash -c","/dev/tcp/","import socket","import pty")
| where not(FileName in~ ("python","python3") and ProcessCommandLine has "marimo")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          ParentCmd   = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildImage  = FolderPath,

          SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("python","python3","uvicorn","gunicorn","marimo")
| where ParentProcessCommandLine has "marimo"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("sh","bash","dash","curl","wget","ncat","nc","busybox")
    or ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("/bin/sh","bash -c","/dev/tcp/","import socket","import pty")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername,
          ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, Hash
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Marimo Notebook Server Spawns Shell or Network Utility (CVE-2026-39987)
id: 7f3c2a91-9b5e-4d8a-b6c4-1e7f3a9d2c8e
status: experimental
description: Detects post-exploitation child processes spawned from a marimo notebook process — the fingerprint of CVE-2026-39987 abuse of the unauthenticated /terminal/ws endpoint.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/05/attackers-use-llm-agent-for-post.html
  - https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-39987
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/05/29
tags:
  - attack.t1190
  - attack.t1059.004
  - attack.initial_access
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: linux
detection:
  parent_marimo:
    ParentImage|contains:
      - 'python'
      - 'uvicorn'
      - 'gunicorn'
    ParentCommandLine|contains: 'marimo'
  child_shell:
    Image|endswith:
      - '/sh'
      - '/bash'
      - '/dash'
      - '/curl'
      - '/wget'
      - '/ncat'
      - '/nc'
  child_cmd_markers:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - '/dev/tcp/'
      - 'bash -c'
      - 'import socket'
      - 'import pty'
  condition: parent_marimo and (child_shell or child_cmd_markers)
falsepositives:
  - Notebook author legitimately running shell commands inside the marimo kernel (treat as anomaly worth review)
level: high
source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:EXECVE (@process.parent.name:(python OR python3 OR uvicorn OR gunicorn) AND @process.parent.command_line:*marimo*) AND (@process.executable.path:(*/bin/sh OR */bin/bash OR */bin/dash OR */usr/bin/curl OR */usr/bin/wget OR */usr/bin/nc OR */usr/bin/ncat) OR @process.command_line:(*"/dev/tcp/"* OR *"bash -c"* OR *"import socket"*))
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ParentBaseFileName=/^(python|python3|python3\.[0-9]+|uvicorn|gunicorn)$/i
| ParentCommandLine=/marimo/i
| (ImageFileName=/\/(sh|bash|dash|curl|wget|nc|ncat|busybox)$/i OR CommandLine=/(\/dev\/tcp\/|bash -c|import socket|import pty)/i)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ImageFileName, CommandLine, ParentCommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Processes.process) as cmdline values(Processes.process_path) as image from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.parent_process_name IN ("python","python3","python3.9","python3.10","python3.11","uvicorn","gunicorn") AND Processes.parent_process="*marimo*") AND (Processes.process_name IN ("sh","bash","dash","curl","wget","ncat","nc","busybox") OR Processes.process IN ("*bash -c*","*/dev/tcp/*","*python -c*import socket*","*python -c*import os*")) by host Processes.user Processes.parent_process Processes.process Processes.process_name Processes.process_path | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
[LLM] AWS Secrets Manager GetSecretValue fan-out from multiple egress IPs Actions on Objectives High
Detects the LLM-agent fingerprint of replaying a single stolen IAM credential through a fanned-out egress pool: the same principal/access key calls GetSecretValue on the same secret from 3+ distinct source IPs in a short window — the IP diversification pattern Sysdig saw used to retrieve the SSH private key. Rationale: Targets the article's defining cloud-credential abuse signature: 'replayed them through a fanned-out egress pool to retrieve an SSH private key from AWS Secrets Manager.' The fan-out is the high-fidelity anomaly — legitimate apps call Secrets Manager from a stable set of IPs (NAT gateway, Lambda, EKS pod IP). The Datadog version also pins the five Cloudflare-egress IPs Sysdig observed. Sentinel/Defender empty: schema reference doesn't include AWSCloudTrail and Defender Advanced Hunting doesn't ingest CloudTrail. Cross-checked against: • https://webflow.sysdig.com/blog/ai-agent-at-the-wheel-how-an-attacker-used-llms-to-move-from-a-cve-to-an-internal-database-in-4-pivots • https://thehackernews.com/2026/05/attackers-use-llm-agent-for-post.html
ATT&CKT1555.006 T1078.004
Data sourcesAuthentication
source:cloudtrail @evt.name:GetSecretValue @evt.outcome:success (CIDR(@network.client.ip, 157.66.54.26/32) OR CIDR(@network.client.ip, 104.28.157.50/32) OR CIDR(@network.client.ip, 104.28.162.160/32) OR CIDR(@network.client.ip, 104.28.165.169/32) OR CIDR(@network.client.ip, 104.28.165.251/32))
# log group: /aws/cloudtrail
fields @timestamp, eventName, sourceIPAddress, userIdentity.arn, userIdentity.accessKeyId, userIdentity.type, requestParameters.secretId, awsRegion
| filter eventName in ["GetSecretValue","DescribeSecret","ListSecrets","GetRandomPassword"]
      and not isPresent(errorCode)
      and userIdentity.type in ["IAMUser","AssumedRole","Federated","WebIdentityUser"]
| stats count(*) as calls, count_distinct(sourceIPAddress) as ip_count, earliest(@timestamp) as first_seen, latest(@timestamp) as last_seen by userIdentity.arn, userIdentity.accessKeyId, requestParameters.secretId
| filter ip_count >= 3
| sort first_seen desc
CLOUD
`cloudtrail` eventName=GetSecretValue NOT errorCode=* | stats count dc(sourceIPAddress) as ip_count earliest(_time) as first_seen latest(_time) as last_seen values(sourceIPAddress) as source_ips values(requestParameters.secretId) as secret_arns by userIdentity.arn userIdentity.accessKeyId requestParameters.secretId | where ip_count >= 3 | eval window_minutes = round((last_seen - first_seen)/60, 1) | where window_minutes <= 30 | sort - first_seen
[LLM] SSH private key file enumeration then read (ls id_ed25519* → cat id_ed25519) Actions on Objectives High
Detects the LLM-agent value-handoff pattern Sysdig documented: an `ls -la ~/.ssh/id_ed25519*` existence check followed within seconds by `cat ~/.ssh/id_ed25519` on the same host/user. The list-then-read sequence on the exact same path is a strong indicator of programmatic (agent) operation, not a human reading the file directly. Rationale: Anchors on the exact behavioural fingerprint Sysdig called out as agent-confirmation: 'a cat command to print the contents of a specific file (cat ~/.ssh/id_ed25519) is preceded by an ls command that passes the same file pattern as input (ls -la ~/.ssh/id_ed25519*) to confirm that the SSH Key exists.' The list-then-read within 60s, same user/host, is the high-fidelity tell — humans rarely script this; agents check existence before consumption. Cross-checked against: • https://webflow.sysdig.com/blog/ai-agent-at-the-wheel-how-an-attacker-used-llms-to-move-from-a-cve-to-an-internal-database-in-4-pivots
ATT&CKT1552.004 T1083
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let WindowSeconds = 60;
let ListEvents = DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where FileName =~ "ls"
    | where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("id_ed25519","id_rsa","id_ecdsa",".ssh/id_")
    | project ListTime = Timestamp, DeviceId, ListAccount = AccountName, ListCmd = ProcessCommandLine;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where FileName in~ ("cat","head","less","more")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"\.ssh/id_(ed25519|rsa|ecdsa)(?!\.pub)"
| join kind=inner ListEvents on DeviceId
| where AccountName == ListAccount
| where Timestamp between (ListTime .. ListTime + WindowSeconds * 1s)
| project ListTime, CatTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ListTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, ListCmd, CatCmd = ProcessCommandLine
| order by CatTime desc
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let WindowSeconds = 60;
let ListEvents = ImProcessCreate
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where ActingProcessName =~ "ls"
    | where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("id_ed25519","id_rsa","id_ecdsa",".ssh/id_")
    | project ListTime = TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ListUser = ActorUsername, ListCmd = ActingProcessCommandLine;
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where ActingProcessName in~ ("cat","head","less","more")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine matches regex @"\.ssh/id_(ed25519|rsa|ecdsa)(?!\.pub)"
| join kind=inner ListEvents on DvcHostname
| where ActorUsername == ListUser
| where TimeGenerated between (ListTime .. ListTime + WindowSeconds * 1s)
| project ListTime, CatTime = TimeGenerated,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', TimeGenerated, ListTime),
          DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ListCmd, CatCmd = ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by CatTime desc
source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:EXECVE @process.name:(cat OR head OR less OR more) @process.command_line:(*".ssh/id_ed25519"* OR *".ssh/id_rsa"* OR *".ssh/id_ecdsa"*) -@process.command_line:*".pub"*
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\/(cat|head|less|more)$/i CommandLine=/\.ssh\/id_(ed25519|rsa|ecdsa)(?!\.pub)/i
| join({#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\/ls$/i CommandLine=/\.ssh\/id_/i}, field=[aid, UserName], include=[ls_time:=_time, ls_cmd:=CommandLine])
| delay := _time - ls_time
| delay >= 0
| delay <= 60
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ls_cmd, CommandLine, delay], function=count())

| tstats `summariesonly` min(_time) as ls_time values(Processes.process) as ls_cmd from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name="ls" AND Processes.process="*id_ed25519*" by host Processes.user _time | rename _time as ls_event_time | join type=inner host Processes.user [| tstats `summariesonly` min(_time) as cat_time values(Processes.process) as cat_cmd from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name IN ("cat","head","less","more") AND Processes.process="*.ssh/id_*" by host Processes.user _time | rename _time as cat_event_time] | eval delay = cat_event_time - ls_event_time | where delay >= 0 AND delay <= 60 | table ls_event_time cat_event_time delay host Processes.user ls_cmd cat_cmd

[LLM] LLM-agent shell fingerprint: machine-consumption flags in single command Actions on Objectives Medium
Detects the structural fingerprint Sysdig identified as LLM-agent-driven shell sessions: a single command line combining stderr discard (2>/dev/null), pager-disable (--no-pager / PAGER=cat / unset PAGER / | cat), and the literal '---' delimiter or bounded-output markers the agent uses to chunk results. Two-of-three present in one command line is a strong agent signal. Rationale: Sysdig's third agent-indicator: 'every command is designed for machine consumption, with each command separated by a --- delimiter, along with bounded output captures, disabling the less command, and discarding the error stream (stderr) to minimize noise.' Three independent unusual-for-humans flags in one command line is the rare-conjunction signal. Pager-disable + stderr-discard alone is noisy (sysadmins do this); adding the literal '---' echo cuts FPs sharply. Cross-checked against: • https://webflow.sysdig.com/blog/ai-agent-at-the-wheel-how-an-attacker-used-llms-to-move-from-a-cve-to-an-internal-database-in-4-pivots
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("bash","sh","dash","zsh","sshd") or FileName in~ ("bash","sh","dash","zsh")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "2>/dev/null"
| extend pagerDisabled = ProcessCommandLine has_any ("--no-pager","PAGER=cat","unset PAGER","unset LESS","| cat","|cat")
| extend delimiterEcho = ProcessCommandLine has_any ("echo ---","echo \"---\"","echo '---'","printf '---")
      or ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"\s---\s"
| where pagerDisabled and delimiterEcho
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName in~ ("bash","sh","dash","zsh") or ParentProcessName in~ ("sshd","bash","sh")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "2>/dev/null"
| extend pagerDisabled = ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("--no-pager","PAGER=cat","unset PAGER","unset LESS","| cat","|cat")
| extend delimiterEcho = ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("echo ---","echo \"---\"","echo '---'","printf '---")
      or ActingProcessCommandLine matches regex @"\s---\s"
| where pagerDisabled and delimiterEcho
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: LLM-Agent Shell Fingerprint (Machine-Consumption Flags in One Command)
id: 3d8e1f72-2a4b-4c9d-8e6f-5a7b9c1d2e3f
status: experimental
description: Detects the structural shell-command fingerprint Sysdig attributed to LLM-agent-driven post-exploitation — stderr discard + pager disable + literal '---' delimiter in a single command line.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/05/attackers-use-llm-agent-for-post.html
  - https://webflow.sysdig.com/blog/ai-agent-at-the-wheel-how-an-attacker-used-llms-to-move-from-a-cve-to-an-internal-database-in-4-pivots

logsource:

detection:
  shell_parent:
    Image|endswith:
      - '/bash'
      - '/sh'
      - '/dash'
      - '/zsh'
  stderr_discard:
    CommandLine|contains: '2>/dev/null'
  pager_disable:

      - '--no-pager'

      - 'printf "---'

falsepositives:
  - Hand-written shell scripts that intentionally chunk output (rare)
  - Power users with shell aliases that disable pager and discard stderr globally

source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:EXECVE @process.name:(bash OR sh OR dash OR zsh) @process.command_line:*"2>/dev/null"* AND (@process.command_line:*"--no-pager"* OR @process.command_line:*"PAGER=cat"* OR @process.command_line:*"unset PAGER"* OR @process.command_line:*"| cat"*) AND (@process.command_line:*"echo ---"* OR @process.command_line:*"echo '---'"* OR @process.command_line:*"echo \"---\""*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\/(bash|sh|dash|zsh)$/i CommandLine=/2>\/dev\/null/i
| CommandLine=/(--no-pager|PAGER=cat|unset PAGER|unset LESS|\| cat|\|cat)/i
| CommandLine=/(echo ['\"]?---|printf ['\"]?---| --- )/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, CommandLine, ParentBaseFileName], function=count())

[LLM] Chinese-language LLM planning comment leaked into command stream (看还能做什么) Actions on Objectives High
Detects the specific Chinese-language planning comment 看还能做什么 ('See what else we can do') that Sysdig observed leaking from the LLM agent's internal reasoning directly into the executed shell command stream. Trivial implementation, very high fidelity — this exact string in a command line is essentially zero-FP outside of native-Chinese-speaking ops environments. Rationale: Quoted verbatim from the article: 'a Chinese-language planning comment, 看还能做什么 translating to See what else we can do leaked directly in the command stream when executing a credential search.' This is an exact-string IOC — zero false positives outside of environments with Chinese-language ops/scripts, and even there the precise five-character planning idiom is incongruous in shell commands. Cross-checked against: • https://webflow.sysdig.com/blog/ai-agent-at-the-wheel-how-an-attacker-used-llms-to-move-from-a-cve-to-an-internal-database-in-4-pivots
ATT&CKT1059
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
union DeviceProcessEvents, DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine contains "看还能做什么"
   or InitiatingProcessCommandLine contains "看还能做什么"
   or AdditionalFields contains "看还能做什么"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true
  (ImProcessCreate | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where ActingProcessCommandLine contains "看还能做什么" or ParentProcessCommandLine contains "看还能做什么" | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, CmdLine = ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentCmdLine = ParentProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate"),
  (Syslog | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where SyslogMessage contains "看还能做什么" | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname = Computer, ActorUsername = ProcessName, CmdLine = SyslogMessage, ParentCmdLine = "", Source = "Syslog")
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] .pgpass read followed by parallel SSH burst to internal host Actions on Objectives Medium
Detects the PostgreSQL-exfil chain: a process reads ~/.pgpass (the per-user libpq password file, source of the reused DB password) then within 10 minutes the same user/host opens 5+ short SSH sessions to a single downstream target — the 'eight short SSH sessions against a downstream SSH bastion server' pattern Sysdig described for the under-2-minute PostgreSQL dump. Rationale: Targets the article's lateral-move pivot: 'eight parallel SSH sessions against the downstream server to siphon an internal PostgreSQL database' driven by credentials extracted from .pgpass. The .pgpass-read seed is article-specific (Sysdig explicitly named running cat of ~/.pgpass to harvest the DB password); SSH-burst alone is too noisy, but anchored on a prior .pgpass cat by the same user within 10m, this catches the exact chain without flagging Ansible runs (which use known_hosts, not .pgpass). Cross-checked against: • https://webflow.sysdig.com/blog/ai-agent-at-the-wheel-how-an-attacker-used-llms-to-move-from-a-cve-to-an-internal-database-in-4-pivots
ATT&CKT1021.004 T1552.001 T1213
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let WindowMinutes = 10;
let MinSshCount = 5;
let PgpassReads = DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where FileName in~ ("cat","head","less","more","awk","grep","tail")
    | where ProcessCommandLine has ".pgpass"
    | project PgpassTime = Timestamp, DeviceId, PgpassUser = AccountName, PgpassCmd = ProcessCommandLine;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where FileName =~ "ssh"
| join kind=inner PgpassReads on DeviceId
| where AccountName == PgpassUser
| where Timestamp between (PgpassTime .. PgpassTime + WindowMinutes * 1m)
| summarize SshCount = count(),
            FirstSsh = min(Timestamp),
            LastSsh = max(Timestamp),
            BurstSeconds = datetime_diff('second', max(Timestamp), min(Timestamp)),
            SshCommands = make_set(ProcessCommandLine, 10)
        by DeviceId, DeviceName, AccountName, PgpassTime, PgpassCmd
| where SshCount >= MinSshCount
| order by FirstSsh desc
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let WindowMinutes = 10;
let MinSshCount = 5;
let PgpassReads = ImProcessCreate
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where ActingProcessName in~ ("cat","head","less","more","awk","grep","tail")
    | where ActingProcessCommandLine has ".pgpass"
    | project PgpassTime = TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, PgpassUser = ActorUsername, PgpassCmd = ActingProcessCommandLine;
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where ActingProcessName =~ "ssh"
| join kind=inner PgpassReads on DvcHostname
| where ActorUsername == PgpassUser
| where TimeGenerated between (PgpassTime .. PgpassTime + WindowMinutes * 1m)
| summarize SshCount = count(),
            FirstSsh = min(TimeGenerated),
            LastSsh = max(TimeGenerated),
            BurstSeconds = datetime_diff('second', max(TimeGenerated), min(TimeGenerated)),
            SshCommands = make_set(ActingProcessCommandLine, 10)
        by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, PgpassTime, PgpassCmd
| where SshCount >= MinSshCount
| order by FirstSsh desc
source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:EXECVE @process.name:(cat OR head OR less OR more OR awk OR grep) @process.command_line:*".pgpass"*
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\/(cat|head|less|more|awk|grep|tail)$/i CommandLine=/\.pgpass/
| pgpass_time := _time
| join({#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\/ssh$/}, field=[aid, UserName], include=[ssh_time:=_time, ssh_cmd:=CommandLine])
| delta := ssh_time - pgpass_time
| delta >= 0
| delta <= 600
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, pgpass_time], function={ count() | collect([ssh_cmd]) })
| _count >= 5

| tstats summariesonly=false min(_time) as pgpass_time values(Processes.process) as pgpass_cmd from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name IN ("cat","head","less","more","awk","grep") AND Processes.process="*.pgpass*" by host Processes.user | join type=inner host Processes.user [| tstats summariesonly=false count as ssh_count dc(Processes.process) as distinct_ssh values(Processes.process) as ssh_cmds min(_time) as first_ssh max(_time) as last_ssh from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name="ssh" by host Processes.user] | eval delta = first_ssh - pgpass_time | where delta >= 0 AND delta <= 600 AND ssh_count >= 5 | table host Processes.user pgpass_time pgpass_cmd first_ssh last_ssh ssh_count distinct_ssh ssh_cmds

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"

     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`

    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user

| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60

Malicious NuGet Package as Sicoob SDK Exfiltrates Banking Passwords

Cyber Security News
2026-05-29 12 use cases 4 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

A newly discovered malicious NuGet package masquerading as an official Sicoob software development kit (SDK) has been caught exfiltrating highly sensitive banking credentials, raising serious concerns about software supply chain security in financial ecosystems. The package, published under the name “Sicoob. Sdk,” targeted developers building integrations with Brazil’s Sicoob banking APIs and silently harvested authentication [&#8230;] The post Malicious NuGet Package as Sicoob SDK Exfiltrates Banking Passwords appeared first on Cyber Security News .

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Malicious Sicoob.Sdk NuGet package restore to .NET project · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Outbound traffic to attacker Sentry tenant o4511335034847232.ingest.de.sentry.io · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] PFX certificate read by .NET process correlated with attacker Sentry egress · Crypto-wallet file/keystore access by non-wallet process · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
[LLM] Malicious Sicoob.Sdk NuGet package restore to .NET project Delivery High
Hunts for the typosquatted Sicoob.Sdk NuGet package being restored / cached on developer workstations or CI build agents. Pivots on the literal package name path written under .nuget\packages by nuget.exe / dotnet.exe / msbuild.exe / devenv.exe so we catch first-party developers pulling the malicious dependency before client instantiation triggers credential theft. Rationale: Anchors on the literal package directory name 'Sicoob.Sdk' written into the NuGet cache by the canonical .NET tool-chain. The package name is unique to this campaign and is named explicitly in the article — any hit is high-fidelity evidence of the malicious dependency landing in the org. Cross-checked against the Socket research summarised in the article body and the publisher/account IOCs in the kill-chain block. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/002/

| where ActionType in ("FileCreated", "FileModified", "FileRenamed")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc

title: NuGet Restore of Malicious Sicoob.Sdk Supply-Chain Package
id: a3f1d8e2-7b6c-4a5d-9e1f-2c8b4d6e1a3f
description: Detects file events that drop the typosquatted Sicoob.Sdk NuGet package under .nuget/packages by nuget.exe / dotnet.exe / msbuild.exe.
references:
  - https://cybersecuritynews.com/malicious-nuget-sicoob-sdk/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/05/29
tags:
  - attack.initial_access
  - attack.t1195.002
  - attack.t1199
logsource:
  category: file_event
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_path:
    TargetFilename|contains: 'sicoob.sdk'
  selection_proc:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\nuget.exe'
      - '\dotnet.exe'
      - '\msbuild.exe'
      - '\devenv.exe'
      - '\vsixinstaller.exe'
  condition: selection_path and selection_proc
falsepositives:
  - Internal package cache mirrored from a sanctioned private NuGet feed before takedown
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 (@TargetFilename:*\\sicoob.sdk\\* OR @TargetFilename:*\\Sicoob.Sdk\\*) (@Image:*\\nuget.exe OR @Image:*\\NuGet.exe OR @Image:*\\dotnet.exe OR @Image:*\\msbuild.exe OR @Image:*\\MSBuild.exe OR @Image:*\\devenv.exe)
#event_simpleName=FileWritten TargetFileName=/\\sicoob\.sdk\\/i
| ContextImageFileName=/(nuget|dotnet|msbuild|devenv|vsixinstaller)\.exe$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, TargetFileName, ContextImageFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.file_path="*\\sicoob.sdk\\*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\Sicoob.Sdk\\*" by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.process_name Filesystem.file_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | where like(lower(process_name), "%nuget.exe%") OR like(lower(process_name), "%dotnet.exe%") OR like(lower(process_name), "%msbuild.exe%") OR like(lower(process_name), "%devenv.exe%") | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.file_path="*\\sicoob.sdk\\*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\Sicoob.Sdk\\*" by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.process_name Filesystem.file_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | where like(lower(process_name), "%nuget.exe%") OR like(lower(process_name), "%dotnet.exe%") OR like(lower(process_name), "%msbuild.exe%") OR like(lower(process_name), "%devenv.exe%") | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
[LLM] PFX certificate read by .NET process correlated with attacker Sentry egress Actions on Objectives High
Joins PFX/P12 reads by .NET hosts (dotnet.exe / w3wp.exe / iisexpress.exe) with outbound traffic from the same process to the attacker-controlled Sentry ingest tenant within a short window. This is the exact behaviour described in the article: the malicious SDK opens the developer's certificate file then POSTs the encoded bytes + plaintext password to Sentry during client instantiation. Rationale: Cross-pivots two article-specific facts that have to coincide in this attack chain: (1) the SDK reads a *.pfx file from disk at client-construct time, and (2) it then transmits the encoded cert + password to the hardcoded Sentry DSN o4511335034847232.ingest.de.sentry.io. Joining the events on DeviceId+InitiatingProcessId+5m window keeps FP rate near zero — legitimate .NET workloads almost never beacon to an unsanctioned Sentry tenant immediately after touching a certificate. No Sigma because the detection is a cross-table temporal join. Cross-checked against: • https://docs.sentry.io/concepts/key-terms/dsn-explainer/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1552/004/
ATT&CKT1552.004 T1555 T1041
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
let SentryHost = "o4511335034847232.ingest.de.sentry.io";
let PfxReads = DeviceFileEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where FileName endswith ".pfx" or FileName endswith ".p12"
    | where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("dotnet.exe", "w3wp.exe", "iisexpress.exe")
    | project PfxTime = Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, PfxPath = FolderPath, PfxFile = FileName, InitiatingProcessId, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName;
let SentryConn = DeviceNetworkEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where RemoteUrl has SentryHost or RemoteUrl endswith "ingest.de.sentry.io"
    | where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("dotnet.exe", "w3wp.exe", "iisexpress.exe")
    | project NetTime = Timestamp, DeviceId, InitiatingProcessId, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort;
PfxReads
| join kind=inner SentryConn on DeviceId, InitiatingProcessId
| where NetTime between (PfxTime .. PfxTime + 5m)
| project PfxTime, NetTime, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, PfxPath, PfxFile, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP
let SentryHost = "o4511335034847232.ingest.de.sentry.io";
let PfxReads = DeviceFileEvents
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where FileName endswith ".pfx" or FileName endswith ".p12"
    | where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("dotnet.exe", "w3wp.exe", "iisexpress.exe")
    | project PfxTime = TimeGenerated, DeviceId, DeviceName, PfxPath = FolderPath, PfxFile = FileName, InitiatingProcessId, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName;
let SentryConn = DeviceNetworkEvents
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where RemoteUrl has SentryHost or RemoteUrl endswith "ingest.de.sentry.io"
    | where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("dotnet.exe", "w3wp.exe", "iisexpress.exe")
    | project NetTime = TimeGenerated, DeviceId, InitiatingProcessId, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort;
PfxReads
| join kind=inner SentryConn on DeviceId, InitiatingProcessId
| where NetTime between (PfxTime .. PfxTime + 5m)
| project PfxTime, NetTime, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, PfxPath, PfxFile, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP

[LLM] Outbound traffic to attacker Sentry tenant o4511335034847232.ingest.de.sentry.io Command & Control High
Network / DNS hunting for the hardcoded Sentry ingest hostname that the malicious Sicoob.Sdk package uses as a covert C2 / exfil channel. This catches any host — developer workstation, CI runner, or production .NET app server — that resolves or POSTs to the attacker-owned Sentry project, independent of whether we observed the PFX read in UC2. Rationale: Pure-IOC detection on the hardcoded attacker-controlled Sentry DSN hostname o4511335034847232.ingest.de.sentry.io named in the article. A Sentry organisation/project numeric id is tenant-unique, so any resolution or connection to it from corporate hosts is malicious by definition unless the SOC has explicitly onboarded that tenant. Used Sentry's DSN docs to confirm the o<org-id>.ingest.<region>.sentry.io naming convention. Cross-checked against: • https://docs.sentry.io/concepts/key-terms/dsn-explainer/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1102/002/
ATT&CKT1102.002 T1071.001 T1567
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web.Web
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "o4511335034847232.ingest.de.sentry.io" or RemoteUrl has "o4511335034847232.ingest"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, ActionType
| order by Timestamp desc
DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Name contains "o4511335034847232" and Name endswith "sentry.io"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType, ResultCodeName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",

                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code.
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Endpoint DNS/HTTP contact with seized Asocks/PROXYLIB C2 infrastructure · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
[LLM] Endpoint DNS/HTTP contact with seized Asocks/PROXYLIB C2 infrastructure Command & Control High
Retro-hunts (and goes-forward alerts) any host in the estate that resolved or connected to the three domains tied to the Dutch-seized 17M-device residential-proxy botnet: asocks.com, bproxy.one, lumiapps.io. A hit means the device is — or was — enrolled as a residential proxy exit node by the PROXYLIB/Asocks operator and likely shipped with a stealth proxyware SDK. Rationale: Three domains (asocks.com, bproxy.one, lumiapps.io) were pre-extracted from the article as the seized infrastructure's customer-facing fronts; the LumiApps SDK and bproxy.one are corroborated by the public Lumen/HUMAN PROXYLIB write-ups (proxylib/asocks SDK family). A retro-hunt across DNS + proxy + EDR network telemetry is the only durable signal because the malware ships as a stealth SDK embedded in legitimate-looking apps and exposes no other host-side IOCs. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1090/002/ • https://blog.lumen.com/proxylib-and-lumiapps-when-bonus-features-become-the-payload/ • https://www.humansecurity.com/learn/blog/satori-threat-intelligence-alert-badbox-and-peachpit-and-the-fraudulent-device-in-your-home
ATT&CKT1090.002 T1071.001 T1583.003
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Web.Web Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
let SeizedC2 = dynamic(["asocks.com","bproxy.one","lumiapps.io"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any (SeizedC2)
    or RemoteUrl endswith ".asocks.com"
    or RemoteUrl endswith ".bproxy.one"
    or RemoteUrl endswith ".lumiapps.io"
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Hits=count(),
            Processes=make_set(InitiatingProcessFileName, 25),
            CmdLines=make_set(InitiatingProcessCommandLine, 10),
            RemoteIPs=make_set(RemoteIP, 25)
          by DeviceId, DeviceName, RemoteUrl
| order by LastSeen desc
let SeizedC2 = dynamic(["asocks.com","bproxy.one","lumiapps.io"]);
union isfuzzy=true
 (DnsEvents
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
   | where Name has_any (SeizedC2)
   | project TimeGenerated, Host=Computer, ClientIP, QueryName=Name, QueryType=QueryTypeName, Source="DnsEvents"),
 (CommonSecurityLog
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
   | where DestinationHostName has_any (SeizedC2)
        or RequestURL has_any (SeizedC2)
        or DestinationDnsDomain has_any (SeizedC2)
   | project TimeGenerated, Host=SourceHostName, ClientIP=SourceIP, QueryName=coalesce(DestinationHostName, DestinationDnsDomain, RequestURL), QueryType=ApplicationProtocol, Source=strcat(DeviceVendor,":",DeviceProduct)),
 (ImDnsActivity
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
   | where DnsQuery has_any (SeizedC2)
   | project TimeGenerated, Host=coalesce(SrcHostname, DvcHostname), ClientIP=SrcIpAddr, QueryName=DnsQuery, QueryType=DnsQueryTypeName, Source="ImDnsActivity")
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), Hits=count(),
            ClientIPs=make_set(ClientIP, 25), Sources=make_set(Source, 10)
          by Host, QueryName
| order by LastSeen desc

[LLM] vpmdhaj npm campaign C2 callback to aab.sportsontheweb.net (X-Supply: 1 marker) Command & Control High
Hunts outbound HTTP/DNS traffic to the campaign C2 domain aab.sportsontheweb.net, including the article-unique X-Supply: 1 HTTP header used by Gen-1 stagers when beaconing to /x.php on port 80. Catches both DNS resolution and proxy-visible HTTP traffic. Rationale: Pivots on the article's two highest-fidelity C2 IOCs: domain aab.sportsontheweb.net and HTTP header marker `X-Supply: 1` on /x.php. Domain is campaign-unique; X-Supply header is mentioned explicitly as a proxy/firewall detection marker.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web.Web Network_Resolution.DNS
let C2Domain = "aab.sportsontheweb.net";
let NetHits = DeviceNetworkEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where RemoteUrl has C2Domain or RemoteUrl endswith ".sportsontheweb.net"
    | extend Source = "Network", Indicator = RemoteUrl
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName = InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Indicator, Source;
let ProcHits = DeviceEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where ActionType in ("ConnectionSuccess", "DnsConnectionInspected")
    | where RemoteUrl has C2Domain or AdditionalFields has "X-Supply: 1"
    | extend Source = "DeviceEvents", Indicator = RemoteUrl
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName = FileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine = ProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Indicator, Source;
union NetHits, ProcHits
| order by Timestamp desc
let C2Domain = "aab.sportsontheweb.net";
let DnsHits = ImDnsActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where DnsQuery has C2Domain
    | extend Host = coalesce(SrcHostname, DvcHostname), User = SrcUsername, Indicator = DnsQuery, Source = "DNS"
    | project TimeGenerated, Host, User, Indicator, Source;
let WebHits = CommonSecurityLog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where RequestURL has C2Domain or DestinationHostName has C2Domain or Message contains "X-Supply"
    | extend Host = SourceHostName, User = SourceUserName, Indicator = coalesce(RequestURL, DestinationHostName), Source = "Proxy"
    | project TimeGenerated, Host, User, Indicator, Source;
let WinDnsHits = DnsEvents
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where Name has C2Domain
    | extend Host = Computer, User = tostring(""), Indicator = Name, Source = "WinDNS"
    | project TimeGenerated, Host, User, Indicator, Source;
union DnsHits, WebHits, WinDnsHits
| order by TimeGenerated desc
