Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d07

author: Clankerusecase

    category: process_creation

detection:

            - '\excel.exe'
            - '\powerpnt.exe'
            - '\outlook.exe'
            - '\onenote.exe'
            - '\mspub.exe'
            - '\visio.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'

level: high

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("638788afc4f1b5860a328312caf5895abd5f5632d28a4f2a85b09076e270d15d", "77d92efe7af3547f71fd41d4a884872d66b1be9499eaa637e91eac866911694d", "bfa149694ec6411c23936311a999163ade54d6f38e2f4b0e3cfb8cb67bd7cfaa") or SHA1 in~ ("638788afc4f1b5860a328312caf5895abd5f5632d28a4f2a85b09076e270d15d", "77d92efe7af3547f71fd41d4a884872d66b1be9499eaa637e91eac866911694d", "bfa149694ec6411c23936311a999163ade54d6f38e2f4b0e3cfb8cb67bd7cfaa") or MD5 in~ ("638788afc4f1b5860a328312caf5895abd5f5632d28a4f2a85b09076e270d15d", "77d92efe7af3547f71fd41d4a884872d66b1be9499eaa637e91eac866911694d", "bfa149694ec6411c23936311a999163ade54d6f38e2f4b0e3cfb8cb67bd7cfaa")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("638788afc4f1b5860a328312caf5895abd5f5632d28a4f2a85b09076e270d15d", "77d92efe7af3547f71fd41d4a884872d66b1be9499eaa637e91eac866911694d", "bfa149694ec6411c23936311a999163ade54d6f38e2f4b0e3cfb8cb67bd7cfaa") or SHA1 in~ ("638788afc4f1b5860a328312caf5895abd5f5632d28a4f2a85b09076e270d15d", "77d92efe7af3547f71fd41d4a884872d66b1be9499eaa637e91eac866911694d", "bfa149694ec6411c23936311a999163ade54d6f38e2f4b0e3cfb8cb67bd7cfaa") or MD5 in~ ("638788afc4f1b5860a328312caf5895abd5f5632d28a4f2a85b09076e270d15d", "77d92efe7af3547f71fd41d4a884872d66b1be9499eaa637e91eac866911694d", "bfa149694ec6411c23936311a999163ade54d6f38e2f4b0e3cfb8cb67bd7cfaa")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["638788afc4f1b5860a328312caf5895abd5f5632d28a4f2a85b09076e270d15d", "77d92efe7af3547f71fd41d4a884872d66b1be9499eaa637e91eac866911694d", "bfa149694ec6411c23936311a999163ade54d6f38e2f4b0e3cfb8cb67bd7cfaa"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Charter Communications data breach affects 4.9 million accounts

BleepingComputer
2026-05-29 7 use cases 2 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

The ShinyHunters extortion gang stole personal information from 4.9 million accounts after hacking the U.S. telecom giant Charter Communications in early April, according to data breach notification service Have I Been Pwned. [...]

ATT&CKT1190 T1566

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Vishing-induced Entra ID sign-in from new location/IP after employee call · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] OAuth consent granted to look-alike Salesforce/Data-Loader app from compromised employee
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] ShinyHunters leak-site Charter URI checked from corporate browsing
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Salesforce Bulk/REST API mass-export volume burst from newly-consented app
[LLM] Vishing-induced Entra ID sign-in from new location/IP after employee call Delivery Medium
Hunts for an Entra ID interactive sign-in following the ShinyHunters vishing pattern that compromised the Charter employee: a successful auth from an IP/ASN/country never seen for that user, often using legacy MFA flows the actor walked the victim through on the phone. Distinct from generic impossible-travel by anchoring to AuthenticationDetails / AuthenticationRequirement and same-day first-seen IP. Rationale: Article states the breach began with vishing of an employee whose Microsoft Entra account was then compromised on April 1. Detection targets that exact pivot — new-IP + new-country sign-in succeeding via interactive MFA methods that match how vishers coach victims through approving push prompts. Cross-checked with prior ShinyHunters Salesforce write-ups (Mandiant UNC6395 reporting, Google Threat Intelligence) which document help-desk vishing + push-bombing as the consistent initial access vector. Cross-checked against: • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/voice-phishing-data-extortion • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/004/
ATT&CKT1566.004 T1078.004
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication

let recent = 24h;

let KnownCountries = AADSignInEventsBeta
    | where Timestamp between (ago(lookback) .. ago(recent))
    | where ErrorCode == 0
    | summarize by AccountUpn, Country;
AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(recent)
| where ErrorCode == 0
| where IsInteractive == true

| join kind=leftanti KnownCountries on AccountUpn, Country

[LLM] OAuth consent granted to look-alike Salesforce/Data-Loader app from compromised employee Installation High
ShinyHunters' Salesforce campaign hinges on tricking the vished employee into granting OAuth consent to a connected app masquerading as 'Salesforce Data Loader' or 'My Ticket Portal'. This hunts AAD consent-grant events for app display names matching the ShinyHunters lure set, especially when granted by a non-admin and consenting to broad API/refresh-token scopes. Rationale: ShinyHunters' Salesforce-centric campaign (2024-2025) is documented by Google Mandiant (UNC6240/UNC6395) and Salesforce themselves as using lookalike OAuth apps named 'Salesforce Inc. Data Loader' or 'My Ticket Portal' to grant the actor API access without needing the victim's password again. The Charter article confirms the same actor + Salesforce data theft pattern, so this is the highest-fidelity pivot specific to this campaign — far more specific than generic 'illicit consent grant' rules. Cross-checked against: • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/voice-phishing-data-extortion • https://www.salesforce.com/blog/protect-against-social-engineering/
ATT&CKT1528 T1550.001
Data sourcesChange.Account_Management
let LureApps = dynamic(["Salesforce Inc. Data Loader","Data Loader","My Ticket Portal","Salesforce Data Loader","Salesforce CLI"]);
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("Consent to application.","Add delegated permission grant.","Add OAuth2PermissionGrant.")
| extend AppName = tostring(parse_json(tostring(RawEventData)).ModifiedProperties[0].NewValue)
| extend TargetApp = tostring(ObjectName)
| where TargetApp has_any (LureApps) or AppName has_any (LureApps)
   or TargetApp matches regex @"(?i)(data\s?loader|salesforce.*data|my\s?ticket\s?portal)"
| extend Consenter = AccountDisplayName, ConsenterUpn = tostring(parse_json(tostring(RawEventData)).UserId)
| project Timestamp, Consenter, ConsenterUpn, TargetApp, AppName, IPAddress, UserAgent, CountryCode, IsAdminOperation, ActionType
| order by Timestamp desc
let LureApps = dynamic(["Salesforce Inc. Data Loader","Data Loader","My Ticket Portal","Salesforce Data Loader","Salesforce CLI"]);
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where OperationName in ("Consent to application","Add delegated permission grant","Add OAuth2PermissionGrant","Add app role assignment grant to user")
| extend TargetApp = tostring(TargetResources[0].displayName)
| extend ConsenterUpn = tostring(InitiatedBy.user.userPrincipalName)
| extend ConsenterIp = tostring(InitiatedBy.user.ipAddress)
| extend ModProps = TargetResources[0].modifiedProperties
| where TargetApp has_any (LureApps)
   or tostring(ModProps) has_any (LureApps)

| project TimeGenerated, ConsenterUpn, ConsenterIp, TargetApp, OperationName, ModProps, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] Salesforce Bulk/REST API mass-export volume burst from newly-consented app Actions on Objectives Medium
Detects the data-exfiltration phase of the Charter/ShinyHunters Salesforce theft: a connected app or session generating an abnormal volume of REST/Bulk API queries against Account/Contact objects within a short window. Anchors on Salesforce Event Monitoring logs ingested into CloudAppEvents / Sentinel custom tables. The 42M-record claim implies sustained Bulk API jobs the EventLogFile.API record makes visible. Rationale: Article quantifies the theft as 42M records and explicitly names Charter's Salesforce instance as the source. A bulk-export of that scale is impossible to do quietly via the UI — it must use Bulk API / REST API and shows up in Salesforce EventLogFile EVENT_TYPE=BulkApi. Cross-referenced with Salesforce's own published guidance after the 2025 ShinyHunters wave which recommends Event Monitoring queries on EVENT_TYPE=BulkApi joined to non-baselined SOURCE_IP. Cross-checked against: • https://www.salesforce.com/blog/protect-against-social-engineering/ • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/voice-phishing-data-extortion
ATT&CKT1530 T1567
Data sourcesWeb.Web
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where Application has "Salesforce"
| where ActionType in ("BulkApiRequest","RestApiRequest","ApiCall","ApiTotalUsage","BulkApi2")
| extend Records = tolong(parse_json(tostring(RawEventData)).RowsProcessed)
| extend Object = tostring(parse_json(tostring(RawEventData)).EntityName)
| extend ClientName = tostring(parse_json(tostring(RawEventData)).ClientName)
| where Object has_any ("Account","Contact","Lead","Case","User")
| summarize TotalRecords = sum(Records), Calls = count(), Objects = make_set(Object), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp)
    by AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, ClientName, IPAddress, bin(Timestamp, 1h)
| where TotalRecords > 50000 or Calls > 1000
| order by TotalRecords desc
let SuspectApps = dynamic(["Salesforce Inc. Data Loader","Data Loader","My Ticket Portal","Salesforce Data Loader"]);
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ResourceDisplayName has "Salesforce" or AppDisplayName has_any (SuspectApps)
| where ResultType == 0
| summarize SignInCount = count(), Apps = make_set(AppDisplayName), IPs = make_set(IPAddress), Countries = make_set(tostring(LocationDetails.countryOrRegion))
    by UserPrincipalName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)
| where SignInCount > 50 or array_length(IPs) > 5
| order by SignInCount desc
source:azure.activeDirectory @evt.name:"Sign-in activity" @properties.resourceDisplayName:*Salesforce* @properties.status.errorCode:0
#event_simpleName=DnsRequest DomainName=/(my\.salesforce\.com|salesforce\.com|force\.com)/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName], function=[count(), min(_time), max(_time)])
| count > 500
APPLICATION
`salesforce_eventlogfile` EVENT_TYPE IN ("API","BulkApi","BulkApi2","RestApi") | stats sum(ROWS_PROCESSED) as records dc(ENTITY_NAME) as objects values(ENTITY_NAME) as objs by USER_ID CLIENT_NAME SOURCE_IP _time span=1h | where records > 50000 OR (objects>=2 AND records>10000) | where match(objs,"(?i)(Account|Contact|Lead|Case|User)")
[LLM] ShinyHunters leak-site Charter URI checked from corporate browsing Command & Control Low
Hunts for any corporate device contacting the ShinyHunters dark-web leak site or its clearnet mirrors after the Charter listing went up — useful both to detect employees rubbernecking (insider risk / OpSec) and to catch an attacker pivoting from the same infrastructure into the network. Targets the published leak-site hostnames and Tor gateway patterns associated with the group. Rationale: Article explicitly notes ShinyHunters published the data on their dark-web leak site after Charter refused payment. Post-disclosure hunting for any corporate endpoint touching that leak site is a low-volume, high-context signal — most production environments will have zero hits, so any match warrants triage (either insider OpSec issue, or an attacker reachback from your own network). Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/charter-communications-data-breach-affects-49-million-accounts/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1090.003

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] Web service in container spawning interactive shell (Redis/nginx RCE) Exploitation High
Hunts CVE-2025-49844 (Redis Lua RCE) and CVE-2026-24061 (nginx) post-exploitation pattern: redis-server, nginx, node or java spawning sh/bash/busybox inside a containerised host — the unambiguous fingerprint of RCE landing inside a vulnerable image. Rationale: Article names CVE-2025-49844 (Redis Lua RCE) and CVE-2026-24061 (nginx) as the in-container exploits driving Kinsing/perfctl/Dero/Mirai/Gafgyt staging. Cross-checked against MITRE T1190 page and abuse.ch ThreatFox notes on Kinsing post-exploit shell drop patterns. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1190/ • https://threatfox.abuse.ch/browse/malware/win.kinsing/

[LLM] Container privilege escalation via Looney Tunables, PwnKit, sudo chroot Exploitation High
Detects CVE-2023-4911 (GLIBC_TUNABLES env-var corruption), CVE-2021-4034 (pkexec PwnKit) and CVE-2025-32463 (sudo --chroot/-R) — the exact local-root chain named in the article for Kinsing and perfctl campaigns. Rationale: Article explicitly names CVE-2023-4911 (Looney Tunables, Kinsing), CVE-2021-4034 (PwnKit, perfctl) and CVE-2025-32463 (sudo). Detection anchors on the unique exploit signatures — GLIBC_TUNABLES=glibc. prefix is the Looney Tunables hallmark, sudo --chroot/-R is CVE-2025-32463-specific. Cross-checked against Qualys advisory for Looney Tunables and the sudo CVE-2025-32463 advisory. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.qualys.com/vulnerabilities-threat-research/2023/10/03/cve-2023-4911-looney-tunables-local-privilege-escalation-in-the-glibcs-ld-so • https://www.stratascale.com/vulnerability-alert-CVE-2025-32463-sudo-chroot • https://attack.mitre.org/software/S1180/
ATT&CKT1068 T1548.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where (ProcessCommandLine has "GLIBC_TUNABLES=glibc.")
    or (FileName =~ "pkexec" and InitiatingProcessAccountName != "root")
    or (FileName =~ "sudo" and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("--chroot "," -R /","--chroot="," -R="))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where (ActingProcessCommandLine has "GLIBC_TUNABLES=glibc.")
    or (ActingProcessName endswith "/pkexec" and ActorUsername != "root")
    or (ActingProcessName endswith "/sudo" and ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("--chroot "," -R /","--chroot="," -R="))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

references:

   OR (ImageFileName=/\/pkexec$/i AND UserName!="root")

[LLM] perfctl rootkit — /etc/ld.so.preload write or LD_PRELOAD on root daemon Installation High
Hunts the perfctl userland rootkit footprint named in the article: write to /etc/ld.so.preload, or a long-running root daemon launched with LD_PRELOAD pointing at a non-standard library — both are the canonical Linux process-hiding persistence pattern. Rationale: Article explicitly states perfctl 'install a rootkit that hides the presence of perfctl on the system' after CVE-2021-4034. /etc/ld.so.preload and LD_PRELOAD are the canonical Linux userland rootkit primitives. Cross-checked against Aqua Nautilus perfctl write-up and MITRE T1574.006 page. Cross-checked against: • https://www.aquasec.com/blog/perfctl-a-stealthy-malware-targeting-millions-of-linux-servers/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1574/006/
ATT&CKT1014 T1574.006
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes
union
(
  DeviceFileEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
  | where FolderPath =~ "/etc/ld.so.preload" or FileName =~ "ld.so.preload"
  | where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FolderPath, FileName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
),
(
  DeviceProcessEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
  | where ProcessCommandLine has "LD_PRELOAD="
  | where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("LD_PRELOAD=/usr/lib/","LD_PRELOAD=/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/"))
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType="LD_PRELOAD_exec", FolderPath, FileName, InitiatingProcessFileName=InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine=ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName=AccountName
)
| order by Timestamp desc
union
(
  ImFileEvent
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
  | where TargetFilePath =~ "/etc/ld.so.preload"
  | where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
  | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, EventType, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
),
(
  ImProcessCreate
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
  | where ActingProcessCommandLine has "LD_PRELOAD="
  | where not (ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("LD_PRELOAD=/usr/lib/","LD_PRELOAD=/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/"))
  | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname=DvcHostname, ActorUsername=ActorUsername, EventType="LD_PRELOAD_exec", TargetFilePath="", ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] Container default credential leak — PKP_DB_PASSWORD=changeMePlease and --secret Weaponization Medium
Hunts the exact plaintext credential anti-patterns shown in the article's Dockerfile screenshots: PKP_DB_PASSWORD set to changeMePlease (or any default vendor value) baked into image layers, and processes launched with --secret <value> arguments visible in /proc. Rationale: Article's verbatim code blocks include PKP_DB_PASSWORD, changeMePlease and --secret as plaintext-credential examples (Block 1/2/3 in tables). The Phase 3 citation explicitly calls out passwords-on-command-line being visible in /proc. PKP_DB_PASSWORD is the documented OJS/PKP default — confirmed via PKP project docs. Cross-checked against: • https://docs.pkp.sfu.ca/admin-guide/en/deploy-docker • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1552/001/

| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("vault","sops","kubectl"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine

[LLM] Container-to-container horizontal scan — Dero miner self-propagation Actions on Objectives Medium
Detects compromised containers fanning out to scan adjacent network ranges for additional vulnerable services, the article-described Dero miner self-propagation behaviour. Threshold-based: many unique destinations on a small set of vulnerable-service ports within a short window, sourced from a single container IP. Rationale: Article's Phase 6 citation describes Dero miner self-propagation via infected containers scanning for new targets. Port set chosen for the article-referenced vulnerable services: Redis (6379, CVE-2025-49844), Docker API (2375/2376), nginx-fronted apps (8080/9000), etcd (2379), DBs. cloudwatch_query left empty — container-to-container traffic does not naturally land in CloudWatch CloudTrail/VPC-flow trails in the analyst-pivot shape this UC needs. Cross-checked against Wiz Dero campaign write-up. Cross-checked against: • https://www.wiz.io/blog/dero-miner-attacks-on-kubernetes-clusters • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1046/

[LLM] Container egress to cryptominer pool / Kinsing C2 Command & Control High
Detects post-compromise C2 from containers: outbound connections to Stratum mining-pool ports (3333/4444/5555/7777/14444) or to known Kinsing/perfctl/Dero infrastructure indicators, initiated from a container-resident process (curl/wget/xmrig/perfctl). Domain indicators cross-checked against abuse.ch ThreatFox Kinsing entries and Aqua Nautilus perfctl/Dero write-ups. [LLM] Kimsuky fake AhnLab/nProtect installer spawning regsvr32 with MemLoader.dll Installation High
Detects the Kimsuky HTTPSpy installer chain where nos-setup.exe (fake nProtect Online Security) or astx-setup.exe (fake AhnLab Safe Transaction / ASTx) launches regsvr32.exe to side-load MemLoader.dll, the second-stage DLL that establishes scheduled-task persistence and beacons to C2. Rationale: Uses three article-specific strings together (parent binaries nos-setup.exe / astx-setup.exe + regsvr32 child + MemLoader.dll cmdline). All three named explicitly by ENKI as the Kimsuky HTTPSpy installer chain. Cross-checked against MITRE Kimsuky/G0094 and CrowdStrike's 2025 European Threat Landscape mention of HTTPSpy. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0094/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/05/kimsuky-deploys-httpspy-expands-arsenal.html

description: Detects nos-setup.exe / astx-setup.exe (fake nProtect / AhnLab ASTx installers) spawning regsvr32 to load MemLoader.dll - the Kimsuky HTTPSpy installer chain documented by ENKI in March 2026.
references:

level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @ParentImage:(*\\nos-setup.exe OR *\\NOS-SETUP.EXE OR *\\astx-setup.exe OR *\\ASTX-SETUP.EXE) @Image:(*\\regsvr32.exe OR *\\RegSvr32.exe OR *\\REGSVR32.EXE) @CommandLine:(*MemLoader.dll* OR *memloader.dll* OR *MEMLOADER.DLL*)

[LLM] Fake Webex camera-fix JSE dropper (fix-camera.jse) via wscript / mTSTCv8.mdxm Delivery High
Detects the April 2026 Kimsuky Webex lure where the victim runs an encrypted JScript file fix-camera.jse via wscript/cscript, which uses PowerShell to drop the intermediate downloader mTSTCv8.mdxm before fetching engine.dat / spyInster.dll. Hunts for either the JSE file execution or the unusual .mdxm extension on disk. Rationale: The .mdxm extension is a non-standard Kimsuky-specific artifact named in the ENKI report; fix-camera.jse and mTSTCv8.mdxm are unique enough that any hit is high-fidelity. Combines the JSE delivery vector with the intermediate-downloader filename. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/05/kimsuky-deploys-httpspy-expands-arsenal.html • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0094/

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent

| where EventID == 4688

[LLM] HTTPSpy loader-chain artifacts on disk (cacheMon.dat, engine.dat, spyInster.dll) Installation High
Detects creation of the unique Kimsuky HTTPSpy stage filenames - cacheMon.dat (loader), engine.dat / spyInster.dll (mid-stage DLLs), mTSTCv8.mdxm (intermediate downloader), MemLoader.dll (installer DLL), and fix-camera.jse - regardless of which entry vector dropped them. Rationale: These six filenames are HTTPSpy/Kimsuky-specific and unlikely to collide with anything benign (engine.dat is generic on its own but in combination with the other five becomes a strong cluster). Disk-write detection catches both the installer and Webex JSE chains in one rule. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/05/kimsuky-deploys-httpspy-expands-arsenal.html

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, MD5, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine

[LLM] VS Code Remote Tunnel abuse for covert C2 (code tunnel) Command & Control Medium
Detects execution of Microsoft VS Code's Remote Tunneling feature (code.exe / code-tunnel.exe with the 'tunnel' subcommand) which Kaspersky observed Kimsuky abusing to establish covert C2 without traditional malware. Tunes for non-developer accounts on hosts that do not normally run VS Code. Rationale: Targets the specific 'code tunnel' invocation pattern Kaspersky documented as Kimsuky's TTP. Includes the --accept-server-license-terms / --random-name / serve-web args that distinguish the C2 use from a developer's normal VS Code launch. Also flagged by Darktrace and Logpresso per the article. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/05/kimsuky-deploys-httpspy-expands-arsenal.html • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1219/
ATT&CKT1219 T1102
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("code.exe","code-tunnel.exe","code-insiders.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "tunnel"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("--accept-server-license-terms","--name","--random-name","serve-web"," tunnel ")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688

| where CommandLine has "tunnel"
| where CommandLine has_any ("--accept-server-license-terms","--name","--random-name","serve-web")
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] AppleSeed GPKI directory enumeration / staging Actions on Objectives High
Detects access, copy, or read of files under C:\GPKI - the South Korean Government Public Key Infrastructure certificate directory that the AppleSeed Spy variant (and Troll Stealer before it) specifically targets per Kaspersky's 2026 Kimsuky report. Excludes platform processes that legitimately enumerate the filesystem. Rationale: C:\GPKI is specifically named in the article (Kaspersky / Troll Stealer mirror) as the AppleSeed exfil target. Korean GPKI certificates are tied to government / enterprise identity and have no benign reason to be touched by non-platform processes. Cross-referenced with prior Troll Stealer reporting. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/05/kimsuky-deploys-httpspy-expands-arsenal.html • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0094/
ATT&CKT1552.004 T1005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FolderPath has @"\GPKI\" or PreviousFolderPath has @"\GPKI\"
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileRenamed","FileModified")
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("explorer.exe","msmpeng.exe","mssense.exe","searchprotocolhost.exe","trustedinstaller.exe","sense.exe","sensesc.exe"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, PreviousFolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFilePath has "\\GPKI\\" or TargetFilePath has "/GPKI/"
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileRenamed","FileModified")
| where not (ActingProcessName has_any ("explorer.exe","MsMpEng.exe","MsSense.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe","TrustedInstaller.exe"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, EventType, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] Kimsuky C2 callback to .r-e.kr / .o-r.kr / .n-e.kr dynamic-DNS infrastructure Command & Control High
Detects DNS resolution or HTTPS callbacks to the Kimsuky 2026 campaign C2 set: eight explicit dynamic-DNS hostnames from ENKI plus the broader .r-e.kr / .o-r.kr / .n-e.kr TLD patterns the actor consistently uses. Both HTTPSpy and AppleSeed clusters use this infrastructure. Rationale: All eight FQDNs are ENKI-published Kimsuky 2026 C2 hosts. The .r-e.kr / .o-r.kr / .n-e.kr dynamic-DNS pattern is also documented as a Kimsuky staple by Kaspersky and CrowdStrike across multiple years, so the TLD-wide fallback catches future campaign rotation. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/05/kimsuky-deploys-httpspy-expands-arsenal.html • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0094/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1568.002

DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any (KimsukyDomains) or RemoteUrl endswith ".r-e.kr" or RemoteUrl endswith ".o-r.kr" or RemoteUrl endswith ".n-e.kr"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc

( DnsEvents
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)

  | project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType, Source = "DnsEvents" ),
( CommonSecurityLog
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where RequestURL has_any (KimsukyDomains) or DestinationHostName has_any (KimsukyDomains) or RequestURL endswith ".r-e.kr" or RequestURL endswith ".o-r.kr" or RequestURL endswith ".n-e.kr"
  | project TimeGenerated, Computer = SourceHostName, ClientIP = SourceIP, Name = coalesce(DestinationHostName, RequestURL), QueryType = "HTTP", Source = "Proxy" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] MemLoader scheduled-task persistence after regsvr32 DLL load Installation Medium
Detects the Kimsuky MemLoader persistence step where, after regsvr32 loads MemLoader.dll, a schtasks /create is issued to re-launch the DLL (often referencing regsvr32, the MemLoader path, or AppData/Public stage paths). Article states 'DLL establishes persistence on the host using a scheduled task'. Rationale: schtasks /create alone is too noisy; combining it with the article's specific stage-binary names (MemLoader, cacheMon, spyInster) plus the user-writable AppData/Public stage paths anchors the detection to the Kimsuky chain. Parent exclusion drops admin GUI-driven task creation. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/05/kimsuky-deploys-httpspy-expands-arsenal.html • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1053/005/
ATT&CKT1053.005 T1547
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "schtasks.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "/create"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("regsvr32","MemLoader","cacheMon","spyInster","\\AppData\\","\\Public\\",".dll")
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("mmc.exe","taskschd.msc","trustedinstaller.exe","msiexec.exe"))
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\schtasks.exe"
| where CommandLine has "/create"
| where CommandLine has_any ("regsvr32","MemLoader","cacheMon","spyInster","\\AppData\\","\\Public\\",".dll")
| where ParentProcessName !endswith "\\mmc.exe" and ParentProcessName !endswith "\\TrustedInstaller.exe" and ParentProcessName !endswith "\\msiexec.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @Image:(*\\schtasks.exe OR *\\SchTasks.exe OR *\\SCHTASKS.EXE) @CommandLine:*"/create"* @CommandLine:(*regsvr32* OR *MemLoader* OR *cacheMon* OR *spyInster* OR *\\AppData\\* OR *\\Public\\*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\\schtasks\.exe$/i CommandLine=/\/create/i CommandLine=/(regsvr32|MemLoader|cacheMon|spyInster|\\AppData\\|\\Public\\)/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, CommandLine], function=count())

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"

| order by TimeGenerated desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["995a0a49ae4b244928b3f67e2bfd7a6e", "52f1ff082e981cbdfd1f045c6021c63f", "9fe43e08c8f446554340f972dac8a68c", "8e15c4d4f71bdd9dbc48cd2cabc87806", "65fc9f06de5603e2c1af9b4f288bb22c", "c19aeaedbbfc4e029f7e9bdface495b9", "8983ffa6da23e0b99ccc58c17b9788c7", "a7f0a18ac87e982d6f32f7a715e12532", "f4465403f9693939fe9c439f0ab33610", "5c373c2116ab4a615e622f577e22e9be", "d1ec20144c83bba921243e72c517da5e", "58ac2f65e335922be3f60e57099dc8a3", "f73ba062116ea9f37d072aa41c7f5108", "7e0825019d0de0c1c4a1673f94043ddb", "08160acf08fccecde7b34090db18b321", "94faed9af49c98a89c8acc55e97276c9", "c42ae004badddd3017adadbdd1421e00", "9ca5f93a732f404bbb2cee848f5bbda0", "678fb1a87af525c33ba2492552d5c0e2"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Typosquatted npm packages used to steal cloud and CI/CD secrets

Microsoft Security Blog
2026-05-29 18 use cases 5 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

The Mini Shai-Hulud campaign used malicious npm packages to target cloud and CI/CD credentials across developer environments. This report details the attack chain, detection opportunities, and mitigation guidance to help organizations identify and disrupt related activity. The post Typosquatted npm packages used to steal cloud and CI/CD secrets appeared first on Microsoft Security Blog .

ATT&CKT1059.001 T1195.002 T1204.002 T1219 T1486
Domainsaab.sportsontheweb.net

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] vpmdhaj typosquat npm package install via preinstall hook (node child of npm) · [LLM] Bun runtime download from github.com/oven-sh during npm install (Gen-2 loader) · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Typosquatted npm packages used to steal cloud and CI/CD secrets
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] payload.bin written under node_modules by node process · [LLM] __DAEMONIZED=1 environment marker on spawned process · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Outbound HTTP beacon to vpmdhaj C2 (aab.sportsontheweb.net) · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Cloud metadata service hit (IMDSv2 / ECS) from node process under node_modules · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft)
[LLM] vpmdhaj typosquat npm package install via preinstall hook (node child of npm) Delivery High
Detects execution of the malicious vpmdhaj cluster of typosquat packages during npm install. Anchors on the exact package names published 2026-05-28 plus the preinstall/postinstall/install lifecycle hook tokens carried in the node command line. Rationale: Anchors on the exact package names and lifecycle-hook tokens documented in Microsoft's article (Block 1 in source) plus the Gen-1/Gen-2 stager filenames (preinstall.js, setup.mjs, opensearch_init.js, ai_init.js). Stagers run as a node child of npm during install — pairing process/parent narrows scope to the actual attack path, not generic npm telemetry.
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName in~ ("node.exe", "node", "npm.cmd", "npm.exe", "npx.cmd", "npx.exe")
   or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe", "node", "npm.cmd", "npm.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("preinstall", "postinstall", "npm install")
   or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("preinstall", "postinstall", "npm install")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any (
    "@vpmdhaj", "opensearch-setup", "opensearch-setup-tool",
    "opensearch-config-utility", "opensearch-security-scanner",
    "elastic-opensearch-helper", "search-engine-setup",
    "env-config-manager", "devops-tools", "search-setup", "elastic-helper",
    "preinstall.js", "setup.mjs", "opensearch_init.js", "ai_init.js"
  )
   or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any (
    "@vpmdhaj", "opensearch-setup", "opensearch-setup-tool",
    "opensearch-config-utility", "opensearch-security-scanner",
    "elastic-opensearch-helper", "search-engine-setup",
    "env-config-manager", "devops-tools", "search-setup", "elastic-helper"
  )
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessParentFileName, FolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\\node.exe", "\\npm.cmd", "\\npx.cmd")
   or ParentProcessName has_any ("\\node.exe", "\\npm.cmd")
| where CommandLine has_any ("preinstall", "postinstall", "npm install")
| where CommandLine has_any (
    "@vpmdhaj", "opensearch-setup", "opensearch-setup-tool",
    "opensearch-config-utility", "opensearch-security-scanner",
    "elastic-opensearch-helper", "search-engine-setup",
    "env-config-manager", "devops-tools", "search-setup", "elastic-helper",
    "preinstall.js", "setup.mjs", "opensearch_init.js", "ai_init.js"
  )
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName, SubjectUserName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: vpmdhaj Typosquat npm Package Install
id: 7c2a4f15-e6b9-4c0a-b8e1-9d5cf2143e21
description: Detects npm install / preinstall hook execution referencing the vpmdhaj cluster of typosquat OpenSearch/ElasticSearch packages published 2026-05-28.
references:
  - https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/05/28/typosquatted-npm-packages-used-steal-cloud-ci-cd-secrets/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/05/29
tags:
  - attack.initial_access
  - attack.t1195.002
  - attack.execution
  - attack.t1059.007
logsource:
  category: process_creation
selection_proc:
  Image|endswith:
    - '\node.exe'
    - '\npm.cmd'
    - '\npx.cmd'
    - '/node'
    - '/npm'
selection_lifecycle:
  CommandLine|contains:
    - 'preinstall'
    - 'postinstall'
    - 'npm install'
selection_pkg:
  CommandLine|contains:
    - '@vpmdhaj'
    - 'opensearch-setup'
    - 'opensearch-setup-tool'
    - 'opensearch-config-utility'
    - 'opensearch-security-scanner'
    - 'elastic-opensearch-helper'
    - 'search-engine-setup'
    - 'env-config-manager'
    - 'preinstall.js'
    - 'setup.mjs'
    - 'opensearch_init.js'
    - 'ai_init.js'

[LLM] payload.bin written under node_modules by node process Installation High
Detects the Gen-1 stager dropping the ~195 KB Bun-compiled second-stage binary as payload.bin inside the package install directory beneath node_modules. The combination of filename, parent directory, and node initiating process is article-specific and very high fidelity. Rationale: Block 2 in the article literally is this detection — payload.bin name + node_modules path + node initiator is exactly the Gen-1 drop. Filename is too generic on its own (any backup or game asset could be called payload.bin) but combined with node_modules + node initiator the FP rate collapses.
ATT&CKT1105 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName =~ "payload.bin"
| where FolderPath has "node_modules"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe", "node", "npm.cmd", "npm.exe", "npx.cmd", "npx.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName, FileSize, SHA256,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventType =~ "FileCreated"
| where TargetFileName =~ "payload.bin"
| where TargetFilePath has "node_modules"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("node", "npm", "npx")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSize,
          TargetFileSHA256, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] Outbound HTTP beacon to vpmdhaj C2 (aab.sportsontheweb.net) Command & Control High
Detects the Gen-1 stager's HTTP C2 beacon and stage-2 download from the vpmdhaj-controlled domain. Scopes the connection on the C2 hostname plus node as the initiating process so non-developer traffic is excluded. Rationale: aab.sportsontheweb.net is the only IOC the article surfaces as a Gen-1 C2 host. Scoping on the FQDN (rather than the X-Supply header, which is not consistently captured in standard CEF / ASIM columns) gives a clean, high-fidelity detection that survives across DNS, proxy, and EDR network telemetry.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1105
Data sourcesWeb Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteUrl has "aab.sportsontheweb.net"
   or RemoteUrl endswith "sportsontheweb.net"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
let C2Host = "aab.sportsontheweb.net";
(union isfuzzy=true
  (CommonSecurityLog
     | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
     | where DestinationHostName has C2Host
          or RequestURL has C2Host
          or DestinationDnsDomain has C2Host
     | project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, SourceUserName, DestinationHostName,
               RequestURL, RequestClientApplication, RequestMethod,
               SentBytes, ReceivedBytes, DeviceProduct),
  (ImWebSession
     | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
     | where Url has C2Host or DstHostname has C2Host
     | project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, DstHostname,
               Url, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, HttpMethod,
               HttpRequestBodyBytes, HttpResponseBodyBytes, EventProduct),
  (DnsEvents
     | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
     | where Name has C2Host
     | project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType, ResultCode))
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Outbound Connection to vpmdhaj C2 Domain

[LLM] __DAEMONIZED=1 environment marker on spawned process Installation High
Detects the vpmdhaj stage-2 binary's self-re-entry guard, which sets __DAEMONIZED=1 in the environment of the detached child to avoid double-spawning. This env-var name is unique to this campaign per Microsoft's writeup. Rationale: Block 3 in the article — the __DAEMONIZED=1 string is a unique campaign artifact called out explicitly in Microsoft's writeup as the re-entry guard. The literal string is not a known legitimate environment variable in any common runtime so single-string match is sufficient.
ATT&CKT1543 T1564

| where ProcessCommandLine has "__DAEMONIZED=1"
   or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "__DAEMONIZED=1"
   or AdditionalFields has "__DAEMONIZED"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "__DAEMONIZED=1"
   or ParentProcessCommandLine has "__DAEMONIZED=1"
   or TargetProcessCommandLine has "__DAEMONIZED=1"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername,
          ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine,
          ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine,
          TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] Cloud metadata service hit (IMDSv2 / ECS) from node process under node_modules Actions on Objectives High
Detects the stage-2 credential harvester's queries against AWS Instance Metadata Service (169.254.169.254) and ECS task-role metadata (169.254.170.2) when the originating process is node — particularly when launched from a node_modules path. Pairs the EDR-side metadata fetch with the CloudTrail-side STS/SecretsManager fan-out for correlation. Rationale: 169.254.169.254 (IMDSv2) and 169.254.170.2 (ECS task role) are the exact metadata endpoints the article names. Pairing the link-local destination with a node/bun initiating process is the article-specific anchor; the CloudTrail companion query catches the fan-out across 16+ regions (GetCallerIdentity → AssumeRole → ListSecrets/GetSecretValue) called out as a defining behaviour of the stage-2 harvester.
ATT&CKT1552.005 T1528 T1555.006
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteIP in ("169.254.169.254", "169.254.170.2")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe", "node", "bun.exe", "bun")
   or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "node_modules"
   or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("preinstall.js", "setup.mjs", "opensearch_init.js", "ai_init.js", "payload.bin")
| summarize HitCount = count(), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp),
            ParentCmds = make_set(InitiatingProcessCommandLine, 5),
            ParentPaths = make_set(InitiatingProcessFolderPath, 5)
            by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RemoteIP
| order by FirstSeen desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DstIpAddr in ("169.254.169.254", "169.254.170.2")
| where SrcUsername !endswith "$"
| summarize HitCount = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated)
          by DvcHostname, SrcUsername, DstIpAddr, NetworkApplicationProtocol
| order by FirstSeen desc
title: AWS IMDSv2 / ECS Metadata Hit From Node
id: a7c91d54-2f8e-4b3a-9c1d-5e8f7a3b6c20
description: Detects an outbound connection to the AWS instance-metadata service (169.254.169.254) or ECS task-role metadata endpoint (169.254.170.2) initiated by a node / bun process — a signature of the vpmdhaj stage-2 credential harvester.
references:
  - https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/05/28/typosquatted-npm-packages-used-steal-cloud-ci-cd-secrets/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/05/29
tags:
  - attack.credential_access
  - attack.t1552.005
  - attack.t1555.006
logsource:
  category: network_connection
selection_ip:
  DestinationIp:
    - '169.254.169.254'
    - '169.254.170.2'
selection_proc:
  Image|endswith:
    - '\node.exe'
    - '\bun.exe'
    - '/node'
    - '/bun'
condition: selection_ip and selection_proc
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 @DestinationIp:(169.254.169.254 OR 169.254.170.2) @Image:(*\node.exe OR *\bun.exe)
#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 RemoteAddressIP4=/^169\.254\.(169\.254|170\.2)$/
| ContextImageFileName=/(\\node\.exe|\\bun\.exe|\/node|\/bun)$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, RemoteAddressIP4], function=count())
# log group: /aws/cloudtrail
fields @timestamp, eventName, eventSource, userIdentity.arn, userIdentity.type, userIdentity.sessionContext.sessionIssuer.userName, sourceIPAddress, userAgent, awsRegion
| filter eventName in ["GetCallerIdentity", "AssumeRole", "ListSecrets", "GetSecretValue"]
  and userIdentity.type in ["AssumedRole", "IAMUser", "WebIdentityUser"]
  and (userAgent like /aws-sdk-js/i or userAgent like /node/i or userAgent like /Bun/i)
| stats count() as call_count,
        count_distinct(eventName) as distinct_events,
        count_distinct(awsRegion) as distinct_regions,
        earliest(@timestamp) as first_seen,
        latest(@timestamp) as last_seen
        by userIdentity.arn, sourceIPAddress
| filter distinct_regions >= 5 and distinct_events >= 2
| sort call_count desc

[LLM] Bun runtime download from github.com/oven-sh during npm install (Gen-2 loader) Delivery Medium
Detects the Gen-2 stager's hallmark: an npm-driven node process fetching a legitimate Bun runtime release (v1.3.13) directly from github.com/oven-sh/bun/releases as a loader for the bundled stage-2 payload. The combination of source (npm install) + destination (oven-sh/bun release asset) is the article-specific signal. Rationale: The article names github.com/oven-sh/bun/releases v1.3.13 as the legitimate-but-abused payload host for the Gen-2 setup.mjs loader. github.com is trusted egress so destination alone is too noisy; pairing it with a node/npm initiating process during install lifecycle bounds the FP rate to actual Bun adopters.
ATT&CKT1105 T1218
Data sourcesWeb Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteUrl has "github.com" and RemoteUrl has "oven-sh/bun"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe", "node", "npm.cmd", "npm.exe", "npx.cmd")
   or InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("node.exe", "node", "npm.cmd", "npm.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("setup.mjs", "preinstall", "postinstall", "npm install", "node_modules")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessParentFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Url has "github.com" and Url has "oven-sh/bun"
| join kind=inner (
    ImProcessCreate
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where ActingProcessName has_any ("node", "npm", "npx")
    | where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("setup.mjs", "preinstall", "postinstall", "npm install", "node_modules")
  ) on $left.DvcHostname == $right.DvcHostname
| where abs(datetime_diff('second', TimeGenerated, TimeGenerated1)) <= 300
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcUsername, Url, DstHostname,
          ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
